narrative:
The model determined that you have a 94.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year ranking had the second-largest impact and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. These two performance measures placed you at the very bottom of your class (decile 1 in both years), far below the average ranking of accepted students, who typically sit around the middle of their class.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor. At 3.00 it was slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, but this actually worked in your favor by nudging the prediction a little toward passing. Unfortunately, that modest positive effect was not nearly enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way. Your LSAT score of 29, middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were also less decisive than your academic standing.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to raise that score significantly, or explore schools and programs with different admissions criteria that place less weight on early class rank. Reapplying later with a clearer demonstration of improvement will be your best next step. (248 words)
